summary: A 1970 note on message data types in the early network. It deals with how data in messages might be described or categorised so different computers can interpret it. It is an early design contribution, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This note proposes putting a data-type label at the start of each normal message. The label would help a receiving system decide how to interpret or transform the remaining data.

subtitle: A proposal to reserve the first eight bits of each message for a shared data-type label.

tldr.problem: Programs need a shared way to identify the kind of data in a message so the receiving host can interpret or transform it.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal reserves the first eight bits of each normal message for a type and distinguishes network-wide standard types from host-local types.
tldr.outcome: The RFC proposes a convention but does not establish which data types the network will adopt.

facts.label: Proposed type field
facts.value: First 8 bits of each normal message

today: The unit metadata records RFC 42's status as Unknown and lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. Its text presents a proposal, not a completed standard.

sections.title: A Type Label at the Start of a Message
sections.content:
The authors propose reserving the first eight bits of every normal message for a message data type. Those bits would not be available for user data.

The convention is intended to let a sender and receiver identify how to interpret message contents before broader network languages for describing syntax and meaning are developed. The proposal does not decide which actual types should be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The first eight bits would identify what kind of data follows. The note proposes the label position but does not choose a final list of types.

sections.title: Standard and Local Types
sections.content:
The proposal separates standard types, which have meaning across the network, from local types, which are meaningful to a particular host. It gives two local type classes: MYLOCAL n for type n in the sending host's set and YOURLOCAL n for type n in the receiving host's set.

The note suggests standard type 0 for YOURLOCAL and standard type 1 for MYLOCAL, with a second byte carrying the local type number. Local type 0 would mean user-specified data that is unchanged and unchecked.
sections.plainLanguage: Some type labels would mean the same thing on every host. Other labels would refer to formats defined by the sending or receiving host.

sections.title: Translation Programs
sections.content:
The authors propose two system programs, called X and Y, to insert, inspect and remove type information. They could also transform data, for example by changing character sets or number formats.

The authors suggest that these programs might later use tables that users could specify, so adding a data representation would not always require changing X or Y.
sections.plainLanguage: Two helper programs would read the label and convert data when needed. A table could tell them how to handle additional formats.

sections.title: Possible Type Values
sections.content:
Possible standard types include YOURLOCAL, MYLOCAL, U.S. ASCII, EBCDIC, Mod 33 TTY ASCII, translation-table operations and a network-standard graphics message. These are examples, not a declaration that the network has adopted them.

Possible local types include local character sets and graphics messages used by specific displays or systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The note lists text and graphics formats as possible labels. Hosts could also define local types for their own character sets or graphics messages.
